inline.s: Thought is the root of delusion, which bores through emptiness each day. Search out its source with care: it hides in unawareness. Once aware, one is no longer deluded; delusion stilled, reality appears. In utmost sincerity without pause, one's goodness deepens and grows.
Inscription on Cultivating the Self

Desires that merely serve the body are the root of self-indulgence; the bewitchment of wine and lust is a pitfall that ruins the self. If one is lost to desire and does not turn back, body and mind will find no firm ground, and this life will have been passed in vain.
Inscription on Ordering the Household

The key to ordering a household lies in thrift and diligence alone. Where righteousness and propriety abound, quiet simplicity grows mellow of itself. Thrift and diligence are handed down through the family; quiet simplicity steadies the will. This is the secret by which sages and worthies conduct themselves in the world.
Inscription on the Six Wondrous Sites, with Introduction

The master of Snowy Peak built his hut beneath the Chaoyang Peak of Shuangjing. The thousand peaks stand like fingers, so he named the place Thousand Fingers. The peak before it clasps the hut closely, curving round like a horn, and I named it Qilin Horn, meaning also that it stands alone. Before the hermitage lies a pool that the local people call Inkstone Washing, for Dongpo thrice roamed this mountain; hence the name is attached to him as a hidden tribute. I changed it to Coming Moon, for the ancients likened the Way to this: once the pool is made, the moon comes of itself. Above the pool stands a studio, which I inscribed Washing the Moon, as a likeness of mind and object. Behind the studio is a spring whose flavor is sweet, cold, and mellow, and I titled it Surpassing Milk. For the ancient sages said that the water at the beginning of the kalpa tasted finer than milk, since it came from the vajra ground; the water on this summit must rise from a deep source, and so it may serve as a likeness of the lineage of the Way, by which one may know its root. Behind the hermitage stands a rock that I named Great Rest, meaning this is a true aranya, a place of genuine practice, a field of quiescence, a site of great repose. These scenes are natural, and so I titled them the Six Wondrous Sites; and at the head of the scroll I wrote: Six Penetrations, Four Reaches, wishing that those within these scenes, however old, might not be bound by wonder. One must simply take away both sides; hence I said reaching and penetrating. Then I made an inscription for each by hand, to record that they be not forgotten. They are not to be met as mere scenery, nor do they fall into words or thought; the host and guest must each attain them for himself.
Thousand Finger Hermitage

A thousand peaks stand erect, pointing straight at this hut; the hut is like space, utterly without a screen. Ask the master within the hut: he neither leaves nor enters. Should one come to call on him, there is only a shout in the void.
Qilin Horn Peak

A herd goes galloping and leaping, yet one qilin is content by itself. What the qilin prizes above all is its single horn, standing alone. A slab of rock is like a qilin, ten thousand trees like its fur; how laughable are those who ride it, never moving a hair.
Coming Moon Pool
The moon never came, nor does the water go; all at once they meet, and no one knows why. The sky beneath the water, the moon within the pool: the marks of coming and going cannot be spoken of at all.
Washing the Moon Studio

The moon has no dust to begin with, the water is clean of itself; from what place should it be washed? Seek it and you cannot find it. The moon falls into the water, the water holds the moon's reflection; a pity that the beholder, in his fevered dream, has not yet awakened.
Surpassing Milk Spring

To pick milk out of water, one must be a goose king; here no picking is needed, only skill in tasting. It is not yet permitted to enter the mouth; one must first know the flavor. Only those who know the flavor drink and are drunk in heart.
Great Rest Rock

A rock is not skilled at running, so why should it need to rest? The greatest rest is rooted in quiescence itself. Sit cross-legged here, unmoving, unshaken, and put forth the broad, long tongue while the pine wind howls through the night.
Inscription on the Prajñā Pavilion, with Preface

The pavilion takes its name from the reading of this sutra. It was the dwelling of the Wumen laymen Zhu Lu and Wang Zaigong. Lu was a remarkable scholar; Zaigong passed the provincial examinations and served as commandant of the prefecture, yet he scorned carriage and cap, abandoned wife and children, and went into retreat on Mount Tianmu. Before long he came again to Shuangjing and stayed in this pavilion, reading the Prajñā Sutra, and greatly awakened. I came from Mount Nanyue and, through the final karmic circumstances of Master Dahui, arrived at this mountain. When the layman saw me he rejoiced and took up the duties of a disciple. I sighed and said: without great strength and a delight in the joy of quiescence, how could one cast off the dust of entanglement at once and come to this? So I named Zhu Great Strength, and Wang Great Cover, and inscribed his pavilion Prajñā. Then I made an inscription to record it, saying:

How startling, this pavilion: bright and utterly transparent, inside and out laid bare, with nothing at all to bind or cling to. At the gates of the six senses all is perfect and void, and world and beyond-world are cast aside together. The flavor of this pavilion is calm, still, silent, and vast; its master within is at ease in body and mind. All the dust of feeling is a bonfire of tiny embers. Ask what this Dharma gate is called: its name cannot be spoken.
Inscription on the Vaiśālī Chamber, with Preface

The layman Guan Juexian grew up in Wumen. He took refuge in the Three Jewels early, kept no wife or children, and gave no thought to livelihood; he built only a single room and named it Vaiśālī, that he might welcome the ten directions. Since there was no Dharma he could speak, he made fragrant rice his Buddha-work. The old monk passed by his chamber, and so he asked me for an inscription. The inscription says:

The city of Vaiśālī is firm and densely sealed; though he dwells amid the marketplace, no trace of dust remains. Within it is a layman who keeps to a single room alone; the door lets in no wind, the six windows are empty and still. Only the ten directions gather like clouds from time to time. To those who ask the Dharma he gives only silence. The fragrant rice is not invited, but eaten as conditions come; no seat is borrowed, the open ground serves as a mat. All that exists is screened away, not a speck of dust is set up. Body and mind are both forgotten, the world is tossed aside together. Ten thousand burdens are all relinquished, all conditions suddenly stilled. To be in the dust and yet beyond it: this is foremost.
Inscription on the Iron Ruyi, with Introduction
When I took leave of Shuangjing, the master of Snowy Peak offered an iron ruyi together with an incense casket. Moved by this, I wrote an inscription.

This ruyi here speaks in place of my mind and mouth; since I cannot speak, I borrow your fine roar. Your words are not nonexistent, my Dharma is not existent; the two being apart, not even the one is held. Only the fragrance of the Dharma-body is paired with you. Trusting to this vajra, it is handed down unperishing.
The Collected Dream Wanderings of Old Master Hanshan, Volume Thirty-Seven
Verses on Mind-Only

Pure, wondrous, beyond conception, the perfect and true mind is vast and endowed with awesome power, manifesting immeasurable things. Its essence is free of every stain, yet it does not forsake the conditions of defilement and purity; in the world and beyond the world it brings all good karma to fulfillment. All karma is like a flower in the sky, from the first having nothing whatsoever; because there is nothing whatsoever, it is said to be true and eternal. One who understands well that the nature of karma is empty is not deluded by magical tricks, clings to nothing and rejects nothing, and contemplates reality in accord with the truth. Where it arises is the unborn; at the very thought it is empty and still, utterly without before or after. A single thought may be Mount Sumeru, yet motion and stillness are equal and thus. The wind of circumstance does not move it; quiescent and wondrous is its constant bliss. Pure as a lotus flower that enters deep into the mire yet is unstained by the dust of the world, one who holds this wish-fulfilling pearl lacks nothing whatever he seeks. Its divine light illumines the darkness, awakening all sentient beings everywhere.
Verses on Dwelling in the Mountains

I ask the people of the mountain: what joy is there in dwelling here? Three bowls of gruel a day, and stretching out both legs to sleep; a flat rock for a Chan bed, cloud and mist for a coverlet; a light breeze stirs the secluded pines and discloses the meaning of the coming from the West. I brush away the flowers in the clouds and scrape off the film from my eyes. A single thought cuts off center and edge, utterly without before or after. Waking, both eyes are empty, and I look back on the things of dream. Scooping at the moon beneath the water only turns to dull obstruction. Cast off both ordinary and sage, and one is freed from the burden of a mother's birth. To bring not a single thing along is still the second principle. Break through the barrier of no-affairs, and only then is the plan to dwell in the mountains fulfilled.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Daze, who thrice crossed the mountains and seas to pay his respects

For whom have you come ten thousand li, and what is it you have come for? Fumbling for your toes inside your boot, you find them nowhere but where they are. If you seek outside yourself, you will walk to the ends of the earth. Coming and going, coming again: this Dharma has never abided anywhere. Ask the monks of Caoxi whether bodhi can have a tree; if you do not gain a single branch, you have wasted the cloth you sold.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Dao Maiyuan

In Chan practice there is no secret formula; what matters is that birth and death be urgent. Birth and death hang at your eyebrows, and thought after thought must never lapse. Lift up the vajra ring, and make your spine strong as iron. Strive onward and press ahead, until the root of the life-force is cut off. Deluded thoughts suddenly vanish, and body and mind are cast aside on the spot. To see the original person is like driving a peg into empty space. Shatter the black lacquer barrel: only then is there great rest.
Inscribed on a Picture of the Ganges, shown to the Chan practitioner Hengyi Lin

The Buddha dwelt on the bank of the Ganges and constantly taught the Dharma facing the river; when he came to a point beyond thought, he used the river's sands as a likeness. Yet even the vast number of those sands does not exhaust the Buddha's meaning; only this Dharma-body reveals the true sense. The Dharma-body never changes, and its nature does not shift as it flows along. Though all manner of filth surrounds it, its essence is forever pure; even when the fire at the kalpa's end burns, its ultimate substance is not destroyed. Therefore the Dharma-body is constant, and self-nature has neither birth nor death. When a son of the Buddha understands this sense and awakens to the body of self-nature, then like the sands of the Ganges his nature is forever one through endless kalpas. This is called the vajra ground; may the Buddha's children dwell there well.
Verses on Contemplating Conditions

Contemplate closely: this body, from beginningless time, arises wholly from inverted deluded thought; it turns through the six realms amid the painful paths, and its nature returns to the human and heavenly states for measureless kalpas. Deluded thoughts never cease, and suffering has no shore; deluded objects are not emptied, and karma is like the sea. If for a single thought one turns the light back for a moment, that very instant one is set upon the other shore. Accumulated deluded karma rises like Mount Sumeru; self and other, right and wrong, are hard and solid in their suffering, forming the iron encircling barrier of birth and death, from which a hundred kalpas and a thousand lives cannot escape. The cauldron of boiling water and the furnace of coals were never there at all; they arise only from a single thought of anger. If at the point where it arises one dissolves it, then in the fire the golden lotus is true liberation. The states before one are like flowers in the sky, not to be likened even to mirror images or water-moons. The people of the world, deluded and confused, lack the eye of wisdom and mistake them for real, seeing them inverted. They foolishly take the four elements as the body and the six consciousnesses and three poisons as their masters, never knowing their own greed and anger and pride, but wildly chasing after the painful paths. When self-nature is pure, that is Amitābha; when the six dusts do not stain, that is the lotus land. When not a single thought arises, birth and death are empty, and in daily life before one's eyes is the true Land of Utmost Bliss.
On Reciting the Buddha's Name

Reciting the Buddha's name is meant to transcend birth and death, yet first one must know the mind of birth and death. Foolish craving is the very root of birth and death; unless that root is pulled out, liberation is hard. Foolish craving is itself the mind that recites the Buddha's name, so use that recitation to cut off foolish craving. If foolish craving can be cut off thought after thought, then mind after mind Amitābha appears in full. This very practice is true diligence, and not a single thought may be forgotten for a moment. The Pure Land lies within the pure mind; do not look for it elsewhere.
Verses on Perfect Brightness, shown to Bi Yisu, who had lost his sight

The mind's light, perfect and bright, is boundless by nature; it is only that the eye is blocked by floating dust. Across a sheet of paper one cannot see outside things, yet turning inward, who has ever seen his own organs? It is like the white sun shining in the sky while a man sits in a dark room as though born blind; the man in the dark also has two eyes, so why do they not meet the sunlight? These four elements of mine are like a thatched hut, and the mind within the body is a bird in a cage. Who can tear away the thatch and seal, when the light shines without end? If one can see for oneself that the mind's light is full, then clearly and constantly bright, one need not use the eyes. This is the light without birth or death, which does not turn and flow with the four elements. How fortunate you are that Heaven has taken pity on you, specially drawing out the obstruction so the heavenly light is whole. You need not complain in broad daylight that you cannot see; it is only like sleeping at night with eyes intact. With eyes intact in night's sleep it is just so: the mind's light, perfect and bright, is simply itself. If one is free of bright and dark and sees one's own mind, this perfect brightness bursts forth at once and transcends birth and death. Who in all the world knows the good of having no eyes? People of old once regretted that they had not gone blind sooner: casting off the four elements at once, the light is whole, and this is our family's wish-fulfilling treasure.
Climbing Kunshan, shown to the companions of my outing

In the city of Kunshan stands a fist of rock, very like Sumeru held in a mustard seed. I came with my staff and climbed it once, and entered at once into the eye of a gnat. When people of the day look up, suddenly it is gone, and the four assemblies all cry out in alarm. Hurrying over to question the man in the void, he simply points out what was there before.
Tan was crushed by a falling beam, and this verse was shown to him

A roof beam collapsed and crushed Tan; yet crushed by it, why did Tan not die? Had the beam reached the body, the body would have shattered; had the body reached the beam, the beam would not have been spared. Since the two did meet, why were they not at odds? Let me ask the reason why they were not at odds. The states before your eyes are not like that beam; why should Tan first be so frightened? And if he would not be frightened, let him watch a cornered dog leap the wall.
Shown to Fu Zhi, styled Benming, who cultivates the Pure Land

Simply contemplate the single phrase Amitābha Buddha, keeping it unbroken in the mind thought after thought. If each thought can be most clear, then you meet Amitābha face to face. Only think that the Pure Land is before your eyes, and in daily use nothing whatever is lacking. The Buddha land is wholly gathered within a single thought, and that is the true skillful means for rebirth there. Only, in the moment of clear awareness, one must not give rise to views of difference.
Contemplating the Body

This body is like a water bubble, briefly appearing and not for long. The foolish child takes it for a pearl, yet cupping it in his hands he cannot fill them. How much more, within it, does much greed become a swamp of sin. Only when seen with the eye of wisdom is it found to hold nothing at all.
Contemplating the Mind

This mind has no form at all; look for it and it cannot be seen. Arising and ceasing have no beginning or end, swift as lightning in the sky. Deluded thoughts chase after the toils of dust, like a thirsty deer racing toward a mirage. How one sighs for the people of past and present, who all suppress what is noble and make it base.

The sea of illusion is shoreless and without end; when will the toil of dust and deluded thought ever cease? Know that the marks of the world are lightning in the sky, and believe that human life is foam upon the water. Only gather the one mind and return to the Pure Land, relying wholly on the ten thousand practices as true cultivation. Whatever lies before you is the road of bodhi, and thought after thought you ever board the boat of prajñā.
Shown to the old monk Wuxiang

When I first met you, you were past sixty; ten years have passed since we parted, and how do you fare now? Time is limited, so awaken again and again; deluded thoughts are boundless, so cut them off thought after thought. The lotus of the Pure Land is watered by the water of Chan; the weeds of craving in the mind's field are hoed by the knife of wisdom. A hundred thousand kalpas have all been passed in emptiness; do not let this life drift into vanity again.
Shown to Shen Shengchengde: Two Poems
A man who sleeps in damp must sicken, yet the loach thrives only there. Each creature's nature has what suits it; why grieve or rejoice at pain and joy?
Things hold nothing to be desired; it is people who desire them of themselves. Sweet and bitter differ in flavor, yet the addict thinks his is wondrous.
Shown to the Layman Liuyi: Two Poems
The affairs of the world are suddenly like a dream, and human feelings are empty as clouds. Who knows that within the dusty marketplace, a still mind is already apart from the crowd?

Though one's traces draw near, how could one go against the world? When the mind is empty, what does it matter whether one is at home? Only look at the muddy water: from it, clear and bright, the lotus rises.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Puwen
You did not shrink from the hardship of a pilgrim's road, crossing mountains and rivers for ten thousand li. Now you have come to the road of Caoxi: who will repay you the money you did not borrow?
Shown to the Chan practitioner Gui of Jinshan: Three Poems
White hairs come, and care is hard to undo; the red dust road does not open. Though the body dwells within the realm of men, the mind is among ten thousand mountains.
Day after day amid the toil of dust, morning after morning in the field of like and dislike, I know not for what affair I busily labor for others.
The sea of suffering is deep beyond a bottom, and the affairs of this floating life have their limit. I know not, within the three realms, where my true home lies.
To Benhun, a Chan Practitioner
Sitting alone among a thousand peaks, too idle to don the hundred-patch robe, I quietly listen to the sound of flowing water and watch the white clouds drift at leisure.
Shown to Ben'ang, styled Fuwu
Where there is a self, one is sure to exalt oneself; pride leans upon temper. Bow down until you reach no-self, and you enter at once the land of coolness.
Shown to Huishan, styled Sea Moon
The great sea gathers all treasures, yet what holds it up is coral alone. The bright moon comes and goes in its time, cool and bright together with the night pearl.
Shown to the Chan practitioner Jingtang
One bowl and a lone staff; across three mountains he forms many conditions. A single drop of water from Caoxi repays the whole price of his straw sandals.
Shown to the student Liu on the Four Rests
To savor one flavor and always be content: much seeking is always a fault. Eat greens and drink water; in this alone one's life is complete.
The Eight Scenes of Bodhi Hermitage, with Introduction
The hermitage stands at Shimen in Jiahe, built by the layman Yan Shengsheng as a quiet dwelling for Master Zhihe Xing. Passing this way on my road to Mount Jing, I therefore wrote these inscriptions.
Bodhi Mountain
Without coming to Bodhi Mountain, how could one know the Bodhi realm? Only the people of the mountain, forgetting words, examine themselves in silence.
Jade-Green City
Verdant green encircles the Dharma city, just like a vajra ring: neither buddha nor māra may enter, and within it all is utterly empty.
An Ancient Image of Guanyin
Guanyin has her before and after, but the Dharma-body has no present or past. Because her mind is cut off from coming and going, she can forever relieve suffering.
Arhat Pine
Tall and upright stands the solitary pine, stately as an arhat's true form. If you would ask about the mind of nirvāṇa, look to the bright moon rising on the branch.
Lotus Bay
The lotus grows in a bay of mud, yet its nature is fragrant and pure by itself. Behold the one within the flower, sitting upright, speaking no word.
Life-Releasing Pool
A single mind of the unborn fully reveals the place of releasing life, causing all the scaly and shelled kind to tread the path beyond birth.
Bubble-Born Stupa
The bubble born was never born; the bubble burst was never destroyed. There remains only the seamless stupa, lighting the bright moon in the cold sky.
The Soap-Berry Tree
By affliction one can remove affliction; the soap-berry tree loves to grow. Seeing these soap-berry beads, one at once gives rise to the thought of leaving affliction behind.
Dwelling in the Mountains, Shown to the Assembly: Twenty-Five Poems
Sitting alone with a censer of incense, free and untroubled, ten thousand cares forgotten; quietly I watch the ants below the steps and wonder for whom they busy themselves after all.
Still and silent, apart from knowing and perceiving; bright and clear, with seeing and hearing dissolved. In the third watch, the moon beyond the sky; a single patch of cloud on the ridge.
The affairs of the world are a game of chess, every move contending for victory. Before black and white are divided, how many can be awake to it?
Within the treasury of pure brightness, a single thought suddenly arises, and the boundless sea of birth and death all comes into being from it.
The road of red dust is longer still; the green mountains are never idle. I ask those who come and go: who knows the good of the mountain?
The deep blue lotus, dwelling in mud yet unstained; the mind that clearly transcends the world is snow within a crystal cup.
The puppets come on stage at night, and the audience sighs with delight. Only in the heart of drunkenness could one bear it; it is hard to keep a sober eye upon it.
The four elements gather as conditions meet, and delusion divides them into fair and foul. Look at this phantom man: where do his feelings and consciousness come from?
A mote of dust contains a world; if you do not believe it wholly contains one, do not say the mote is small, but know that the world is empty.
On the road before the withered-wood cliff, the traveler comes and loses his way. He should climb another peak and rise one more rung of the ladder.
The bank tree splits the sheer cliff, the withered vine hangs over the ancient well. How can it bear the gnawing of the two mice, much less the assault of the rushing stream?
In the blazing house of fire there is no avoiding the heat of affliction. In the moment a single thought is set down, one attains at once the land of coolness.
The whole world wants much and seeks it; the more one seeks, the more affliction is born. Only the mind content with enough is the wish-fulfilling treasure.
The Pure Land appears from mind alone; the lotus is the fragrance of the nature-ground. If before your eyes it is never obscured, then this very place is the West.
Deluded thought is the realm of sinking and drowning; the purified mind is the place of liberation. When the light is turned back and shines within, face to face one bows to the King of Emptiness.
Chasing and racing after the mirage, step by step one enters the pit of fire. If one can open a single eye, in that instant one is the unborn.
The roads of the world are full of entanglements; empty fame is what binds a man most. Only when the thread at one's heel is cut is one permitted to leave the red dust.
In mountain forests there is much to delight the spirit; yet how many can savor the stillness? Until one reaches the place of true rest, it all ends as talk on the lips.
The mark of self is truly hard to break; the faults of others are very easy to find. A whole life spent in idle fault-finding comes in the end to nothing at all.
The self-nature is the buddha of innate suchness, yet it is all entangled by deluded thought. If one can but see through it once, on the spot one realizes the Golden Immortal.
